what: Figure Technology Solutions originates and sells consumer loans, principally home equity lines of credit, using blockchain technology to record and transfer them. Its argument is that recording a loan on a shared ledger removes cost and time from origination, servicing and sale to investors.
customers: Homeowners borrowing against the equity in their house, usually through partner lenders and credit unions that use Figure’s technology, and the institutional investors who buy the resulting loans.
money: Gains from originating home equity loans and selling them to investors.
Fees from partners using the platform, and servicing income.
moat: The claimed advantage is speed and cost: a home equity line that takes weeks through a traditional lender can be approved in days, because verification and recording happen on one shared system rather than across several institutions. If that holds, the cost per loan is structurally lower, which in a commodity lending product is the only durable advantage there is.
risks: This is a lending business, so its results depend on credit quality and on being able to sell the loans it makes. Both can change quickly.
Free cash flow of $60.5M against net income of $244.7M is a large gap, which in a lender usually reflects loans held on the balance sheet rather than sold.
The company listed recently, so there is no public record of how it performs through a credit downturn — and home equity lending is precisely the product that performed worst in the last one.
The shares trade at about 27.2 times earnings and 6.9 times sales on a short history.
Ten analysts average a $46.70 target against a $25.84 price, an 81% gap that signals wide disagreement rather than a consensus.
opportunities: Revenue has grown very fast, from $209.5M in 2023 to $506.9M in 2025, with trailing revenue of about $839.6M.

Home equity is a genuinely attractive lending product right now: homeowners have large accumulated equity and will not refinance their cheap first mortgage, so borrowing against it is the only way to access that money.
Cash of $1.2B against $562.9M of debt is a strong position for a lender of this size.
Partner lenders and credit unions using the platform give distribution without Figure paying to acquire each borrower.
watch: Credit performance on the loans originated, and whether they are being sold or retained. A lender’s growth is easy and its credit is hard, and the two become visible at very different times.
view: Figure is a lender with a technology story attached, and the order of those two words matters enormously. The technology claim is that recording loans on a shared ledger removes cost and time from origination and sale — a home equity line approved in days instead of weeks. If true, that is a real and durable advantage, because home equity lending is a commodity product where the low-cost originator wins. The evidence so far is revenue going from $209 million to $507 million in two years, which says the product works and borrowers want it.

The product also arrives at an unusually favourable moment, and this deserves more weight than the blockchain framing. American homeowners are sitting on enormous accumulated equity and are locked into first mortgages at rates they will never see again. They will not refinance, because refinancing means giving up a cheap loan. The only way to access that equity is to borrow against it separately, which is exactly what Figure sells. That is a structural tailwind created by interest rates rather than by any technology.

What I would not do is let the growth or the technology distract from what this is: a credit business. Lenders grow easily and fail slowly. Originating loans is the simple part; the difficulty arrives two or three years later when the loans either perform or do not, and home equity is precisely the product that performed worst in the last housing downturn, because it sits behind the first mortgage and recovers nothing when a house is sold at a loss. Figure listed recently and has no public record through a credit cycle at all.

The gap between the $26 share price and the $47 analyst average is the market and the sell side disagreeing about exactly that. At 27 times earnings on a short history, I would want two specific things before forming a positive view: the credit performance of the vintages already originated, and whether loans are being sold to investors or retained on the balance sheet — because the gap between $245 million of net income and $61 million of free cash flow suggests retention, and retention means Figure keeps the credit risk rather than passing it on.
bull: The lower cost per loan proves structural, homeowners keep tapping equity they cannot refinance into, and partner distribution scales origination without acquisition cost.
bear: Credit turns in a product that sits behind the first mortgage, the loans being retained rather than sold put the losses on Figure’s own balance sheet, and a short public record offers no reassurance.
